title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
content:
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.
A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.
Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant development in the education sector of a major country, providing insight into a high-stakes exam cheating scandal that has consequences for millions of students, and the resignation of the education minister in response, making it a newsworthy story for a public-interest news product.

title: This split in the Republican coalition could transform the electoral map in 2028
content: White evangelical Christians stuck with Republicans more loyally than any other major demographic group in this month’s election. But that unshakeable alliance could present as much of a threat as an opportunity for the GOP as it charts a path toward recovery in 2028. While more than 4 in 5 White evangelicals still cast their votes for the GOP, results from the CNN Voter Poll reveal that Democrats achieved historic breakthroughs among the large majority of voters who don’t identify as evangelical Christians — even in previously red states across the South and Midwest. That stark divergence means the GOP is emerging from this election increasingly dependent on support from White evangelicals — even as they have been shrinking as a share of American society. That dynamic could leave the party stuck between satisfying a religiously conservative base that thrills to President Donald Trump’s polarizing — plus his confrontational culture war politics — and repositioning in ways that might help recapture the swing voters and even soft Republicans who stampeded away from them this month. “The wave is going to push (Republicans) further to the right and just make them dig in even more,” says progressive strategist Michael Podhorzer, the author of an extensive recent study on the role that White evangelicals play inside the GOP . Looking forward to 2028, the stark lesson for Republicans from this year’s thrashing is that while they succeeded in holding evangelicals with a lacerating cultural message against Democrats, those arguments failed to overcome frustrations about the economy, the Iran War, perceived corruption and Trump’s governing style among the much broader universe of non-evangelical voters who have traditionally backed the GOP, especially in red-leaning states. Unless the GOP can significantly reverse the Democratic inroads with those non-evangelical voters, the Electoral College map in 2028 would look radically different — with Republicans suddenly sweating in states such as Iowa, Ohio and even Texas, Kansas and beyond that have appeared securely red, even for many years before the Trump era. As the final ballots are tallied, Democrats are on track to win the national popular vote in House elections this year by about 14 percentage points. That would be the largest margin for either party in a midterm election since the Democrats’ 1974 post-Watergate landslide. Yet Republican support among White evangelical Christians held like a boulder in that torrent. In the Voter Poll measuring preferences for the House , Republicans beat Democrats among White evangelical Christians, 82% to 17%. That exactly matched Trump’s margin among them over Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 election. In the states where exit poll data on Trump’s performance among White evangelicals in 2024 is available, winning Democratic Senate candidates James Talarico in Texas, Jon Ossoff in Georgia, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Roy Cooper in North Carolina all improved slightly over Harris’ 2024 performance, capturing between 17% to 21% of them. In other states with large White evangelical populations, winning Democrats Annie Andrews in South Carolina, Adam Hamilton in Kansas, Josh Turek in Iowa, and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota also won about one-fifth of White evangelical Christians, according to the Voter Poll, which was conducted by SSRS for a consortium of news organizations including CNN. But that meant every Republican in a closely contested Senate race still won at least three-fourths of White evangelicals, with most capturing over four-fifths. Fully 90% of White evangelicals voted against Democrat Scott Colom, who will become Mississippi’s first Black Senator since Reconstruction. That record is especially remarkable given that a substantial majority of White evangelicals also expressed discontent over the economy in most polls, such as the pre-election survey by the Public Religion Research Institute , a nonpartisan group that studies religion and politics. “Their vote wasn’t about the economy; it wasn’t about the war,” said Robert P. Jones, PRRI’s president and founder. “It was a belief in the larger MAGA vision of the country” centered on reversing the cultural and demographic changes since the 1960s. Terry Schilling, president of the social conservative group American Principles Project, agrees that for evangelical Christians, affinity with Trump’s cultural agenda outweighed disappointment in his economic record. “If they had to choose between their pocketbook and God’s law… they are going to protect their values,” he says. The GOP’s problem is that those issues were either not sufficiently compelling or they actively repelled other voters who have supported the party before. Across the 2026 battlefield, Democrats posted head-turning margins among the big majority of voters who are not evangelicals. (According to the Voter Poll, White evangelicals represented about 1 in 6 voters nationwide and voters who are not White evangelicals about 5 in 6.) Eight of the nine Democrats who flipped a Republican-held Senate seat this month won at least three-fifths of all voters across racial lines who did not identify as White evangelical Christians, according to the Voter Poll. (The sole exception was Mary Peltola in Alaska, who carried 59% of them.) Maybe even more striking was the Democratic performance among the White voters who are not evangelical Christians. Especially in Southern and heartland states, Democrats have often struggled among those non-evangelical Whites, who tend to be more conservative, especially on cultural issues, than their demographic counterparts along the coasts or in the upper Midwest. But this year, all nine Democrats who captured a GOP-held Senate seat won a majority of White voters who did not identify as evangelical Christians; even in Southern states, Ossoff, Talarico and Cooper each won at least 56% of them. Perhaps most remarkably, Colom won a 51% majority of non-evangelical whites in Mississippi . Governor races across the South produced similarly striking results. In Alabama, Democrat Doug Jones carried most non-evangelical Whites in his unexpectedly narrow defeat. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms split them nearly evenly in her comfortable win. And maybe most surprisingly, in Texas, newly elected Democrat Gina Hinojosa solidly beat Republican Gov. Greg Abbott by 11 points among those non-evangelical Whites. The results in Texas are especially noteworthy because in no other state has the GOP fused its identity and agenda more fully with the priorities of White evangelical Christians. In recent years, Abbott and the Republican majorities in the state legislature have banned abortion ; severely limited what teachers can say about race, gender and sexuality in the classroom ; and passed legislation requiring public schools to display the Ten Commandments . The Republican-controlled State Board of Education has approved curriculum changes that will require Bible readings in public schools starting in 2030 and describe the Islamic faith in derogatory terms. Abbott and other Texas Republicans have raised persistent alarms about the state’s growing Muslim population . “Texas is right up there at the very top” of states that have incorporated evangelical Christian priorities into public policy, says Rachel Laser, president and CEO of Americans United for Separation of Church and State. During the 2026 campaign, Texas Republicans and their evangelical allies leaned heavily on cultural arguments against Democrats, particularly Talarico, a former Presbyterian seminarian. Republicans pounded voters with ads misleadingly claiming that Talarico supported gender reassignment surgery for minors and denouncing his earlier assertion that God was nonbinary. James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas, says Republicans sublimated their traditional messages about taxes, the economy and immigration to focus overwhelmingly on trying “to portray Democrats … as a cultural threat.” Yet not only did Talarico beat Paxton by a stunning 1.2 million votes, but Democrats swept every statewide office, after not winning any of them since 1994. (Democrats even captured a one-seat majority on the state Board of Education — which will empower them to reverse the curriculum decisions of the ousted GOP-majority board.) While 80% of White evangelicals stuck with Paxton, Talarico made big gains not only with the non-evangelical Whites, but also Latino voters alienated by Trump’s mass deportation program and the state’s growing Asian population, which includes many South Asians offended by the GOP’s pervasive anti-Muslim rhetoric . Voters who identify with no religion matched White evangelicals at around one-fifth of all voters — and they provided Talarico with almost exactly as big a margin as evangelicals gave Talarico, the Voter Poll found . Laser says her group’s private polling shows that Texas voters were recoiling, at least in part, from the GOP’s years-long campaign to lower barriers between church and state. “In states like Texas that has been the bastion of Christian nationalism there is the most energy to fight back,” she says. Henson isn’t as certain most Texas voters were rejecting the state policies that advanced evangelical Christian priorities. In the Voter Poll, for instance, 58% of Texas voters said society has gone too far trying to guarantee transgender rights. But what is clear, he says, is that the cultural issues Republicans were hoping would energize their core voters fizzled. “It was meant as an antidote to the very clear enthusiasm and mobilization problems that Republicans had throughout the cycle,” Henson says. “And it did not work.” To the PRRI’s Jones, the failure of the GOP cultural assault on Talarico encapsulates the GOP’s larger risk. Since the 1990s, White evangelical Christians’ share of the overall US population has fallen from 27% to 13%, according to data from PRRI and the Pew Research Center . In the past few years, Jones notes, that number has stopped declining, but “there’s very little chance they are going to grow” because the share of young adults who identify with that religious tradition has dropped below 10%. Those long-term population trends mean Republicans can’t rely on White evangelicals to increase their share of voters in 2028 — and face the risk they could contract even further. By contrast, Jones notes, the share of Americans who are unaffiliated with any religious tradition has increased to 28% nationally (although it has plateaued in recent years) — and nearly four-fifths of those secular voters backed Democrats this year, an ominous trend for the GOP. Nonwhite Christians are holding steady at about one-fourth of society; but apart from Hispanic Protestants (many of whom are evangelicals), they have not been nearly as receptive to the combative cultural messages that move most White evangelicals. White Catholics and White mainline Protestants have both mostly voted Republican in recent years. But both have also declined as a share of the overall society since the early 2000s-and each moved toward Democrats this year compared to 2024, the Voter Poll found . All these shifts in America’s religious landscape increase the pressure on the GOP in 2028 to appeal to Americans from a broader range of faith traditions — or no faith tradition at all. Yet as White evangelicals shrink in society, Republicans in the Trump era have deepened their identification with the group. In both rhetoric and policy, Trump has melded the GOP’s identity with the militant White evangelical attitudes on all the major issues relating to American identity , from immigration enforcement to gender roles, LGBTQ rights and the role of Christianity in public life. “With Trump, the party has become over-aligned to White evangelical interests,” Jones says. If anything, White evangelicals’ influence may rise inside the GOP after this wipe-out. Heading into this election, Podhorzer calculated that 61% of House Republicans represented seats where the White evangelical share of the population ranks in the top two-fifths of all districts; after the election, he found, about two-thirds of all House Republicans will represent such evangelical-heavy districts. Similarly, just five of the GOP’s remaining 44 senators will represent states with fewer evangelicals than the national average . Schilling says for Republicans it would “be suicide to drop” the conservative cultural positions that attract those evangelical voters. Even amid this month’s rout, he notes, four states passed ballot initiatives barring transgender girls from participating in school sports ; as in Texas, the Voter Poll showed that a majority of voters in almost all competitive states said society has gone too far in promoting transgender rights. But other GOP cultural priorities popular with evangelicals face stiffer opposition. Majorities in almost all competitive states this year said Trump’s deportation efforts have gone too far. Most voters support legal abortion in about four-fifths of the states , including many that have restricted it. While Democrats and their progressive allies believe the GOP’s Trump-era cultural agenda alienates more voters than it attracts, and Republicans believe the opposite, almost everyone on both sides agree on one overriding lesson from 2026: Cultural arguments alone can’t sustain a Republican majority when voters are this discontented about the economy and other issues, such as corruption. “You know what is salient? Filling up your gas tank,” says veteran GOP consultant David Kochel. “You know what’s not salient? I don’t have any trans kids playing on my daughter’s softball team. You can’t make an entire national election about a tiny little thing like that.” Even Schilling agrees that this year’s result show that by 2028 Republicans “have to get an economic message that appeals to these working families that aren’t as religiously motivated.” Maintaining support from White evangelicals may be necessary for any Republican recovery. But 2026 vividly demonstrated it is not sufficient, even in states such as Texas, South Carolina, Iowa and Kansas where they have previously been a dominant force. The harder question for Republicans may be whether the sharp-edged MAGA agenda that solidifies the party’s hold on evangelicals is not only insufficient to win back the voters who rejected them this month — but actively diminishes their chances of doing so.
ranking_reason: The GOP is emerging from this election increasingly dependent on support from White evangelicals — even as they have been shrinking as a share of American society.

analysis.reason: The GOP is emerging from this election increasingly dependent on support from White evangelicals — even as they have been shrinking as a share of American society.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant shift in the electoral landscape, highlighting the potential consequences of the GOP's increasing reliance on White evangelicals, and provides a clear reason for readers to care: the potential transformation of the Electoral College map in 2028.

title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
content:
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government.
The statement said there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Later on Sunday, the health ministry said it had received injured people from another vessel, a commercial ship, that was also targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.
US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.
Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
"Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians."
If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.
As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.
But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.
Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."
Additional reporting by Benedict Garman and Shayan Sardarizadeh
ranking_reason: A routine incident with limited public impact.

analysis.reason: A routine incident with limited public impact.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant incident involving a Russian ship in a Libyan port, with evidence of a suspected drone attack and potential consequences for regional politics and maritime safety. The story has international implications and provides a clear reason for readers to care, making it suitable for publication in a high-value public-interest news product.
